name: Indonesia
summary: The world’s largest archipelagic state and fourth most populous country. It proclaimed independence in 1945, won recognition from the Netherlands in 1949, and moved from Sukarno’s and Suharto’s rule to democracy after 1998.

knownFor.label: Batik (UNESCO)
knownFor.note: Inscribed as Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2009.

knownFor.label: Bahasa Indonesia
knownFor.note: A national language uniting hundreds of ethnic groups.

location.value: The world’s largest archipelagic state, with 13,000–17,000 islands between Asia and Oceania. Area 1,904,569 km² (14th largest).

terrain.value: Volcanic islands (Java, Sumatra) with about 130 active volcanoes, plus Borneo (Kalimantan), Sulawesi and New Guinea (Papua). Highest point Puncak Jaya (4,884 m).

climate.value: Tropical, with extensive rainforests and marine ecosystems that hold some of the world’s highest biodiversity.

resources.value: Oil and gas, coal, nickel, palm oil, timber and rubber. Palm oil and timber accounted for over 40% of deforestation from 2001 to 2016.

disasters.value: Frequent earthquakes, eruptions and tsunamis. The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami devastated Aceh.
disasters.source: Wikipedia: Indonesia (checked 5 Nov 2026); Wikipedia: History of Indonesia (checked 5 Nov 2026)

population.value: 270,203,917 in the 2020 census, and about 290 million in 2026: the world’s fourth-largest population.

urbanisation.value: More than half of Indonesians live on Java. Jakarta is the capital and largest city.

disease.value: Tropical diseases such as dengue fever and malaria remain public-health issues. The COVID-19 pandemic hit Indonesia hard from 2020.
disease.source: Wikipedia: COVID-19 pandemic in Indonesia (not checked in this pass)

migration.value: Government “transmigration” programmes moved people from crowded Java to other islands. They began as a colonial scheme in 1905.

economicBase.value: Services and industry produce most output, with economic activity concentrated on Java. Large commodity exports.

tradeRoutes.value: Sea and air transport connect the islands. Major trade with China, Japan, the US and ASEAN.

wealth.value: The largest economy in Southeast Asia. GDP per person about $5,153 (nominal) or $19,091 (PPP), 2026 estimates.

moneyAndTax.value: The rupiah (IDR). Indonesia was the country hardest hit by the 1997–98 Asian financial crisis, which led to protests and Suharto’s resignation.

inequality.value: Gini 36.8 (“medium inequality”). New Order growth “disproportionately benefited elites, while poverty and inequality persisted”.
inequality.source: Wikipedia: Indonesia (checked 5 Nov 2026) (infobox); Wikipedia: History of Indonesia (checked 5 Nov 2026)

governmentType.value: A unitary presidential republic with 38 provinces, some with special autonomy. The national ideology is Pancasila (the Five Principles).

keyRulers.value: Sukarno (1945–1967). Suharto (acting from 1967, president 1968–1998). B. J. Habibie. Abdurrahman Wahid. Later and present leaders are not named here.
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Indonesia (checked 5 Nov 2026); Wikipedia: History of Indonesia (checked 5 Nov 2026)

succession.value: Direct presidential elections since 2004, after the authoritarian New Order ended in 1998.

institutions.value: The People’s Consultative Assembly (MPR) with the DPR and DPD, a constitutional court, and regional autonomy introduced during Reformasi.

stability.value: An attempted coup in 1965 led to a violent army-led anti-communist purge in which over half a million people were killed (estimates range to about one million). The New Order (1967–1998) followed. Separatist conflicts in Aceh (peace deal 2005) and Papua.

eliteConflict.value: The New Order was marked by “widespread corruption, nepotism, human rights abuses, and the centralization of power”. Corruption remains a challenge.

armyAndTech.value: The Indonesian National Armed Forces (TNI) played a major political role under the New Order. Indonesia has contributed UN peacekeepers since 1957.

majorWars.value: The National Revolution against the Dutch (1945–1949). Konfrontasi with Malaysia (1963–66). The invasion and occupation of East Timor (1975–1999). Counter-insurgency in Aceh and Papua.

territoryChange.value: Inherited the borders of the Dutch East Indies. Took control of West New Guinea (Papua) through the contested 1969 “Act of Free Choice”. East Timor voted for independence in 1999 (independent 2002).
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Indonesia (checked 5 Nov 2026); Wikipedia: History of Indonesia (checked 5 Nov 2026)

alliancesRivals.value: A founder of ASEAN (1967, headquartered in Jakarta) and of the Non-Aligned Movement (Bandung Conference, 1955). Follows an “independent and active” foreign policy.

inventions.value: Developed aircraft (IPTN) and satellite programmes. Industrial growth mainly in manufacturing and resources. Not detailed in the sources checked.
inventions.source: Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c. 1200 (2008)

scienceEducation.value: Colonial schooling reached only a small minority. Mass education expanded after independence. Literacy figures are not stated in the sections checked.

openness.value: Shifted from Sukarno’s nationalist and anti-Western stance to the New Order’s openness to Western investment, then democratic opening after 1998.

communicationTransport.value: Ferries and planes connect the islands; the Jakarta–Bandung high-speed railway began commercial operations in 2023.

religion.value: Islam 87.2% (the largest Muslim population of any country), Christianity 10.4%, Hinduism 1.7% (mainly Bali), Buddhism 0.7% (2025).

languageWriting.value: Indonesian, a standardised form of Malay chosen as the “language of unity” in 1928, plus 729 indigenous languages. Written in Latin script.

artsArchitecture.value: Heritage from Borobudur and Prambanan (8th–10th centuries) to batik, gamelan, wayang and the cultures of hundreds of ethnic groups.

socialStructure.value: Hundreds of ethnic groups: Javanese 40.1%, Sundanese 15.5%, Malay 3.7%, Batak 3.6% and 600+ others (2010).

sharedIdentity.value: “Bhinneka Tunggal Ika” (Unity in Diversity), Pancasila, and the Indonesian language, chosen in the 1928 Youth Pledge.

dailyLife.value: Village houses and city kampongs; rice, tempeh, sambal; mobile phones in daily life.

neighbours.value: Malaysia, Singapore, Timor-Leste, Papua New Guinea, Australia and the Philippines.

ideasReligions.value: A middle power in the UN, G20, ASEAN, the Non-Aligned Movement and the OIC.

colonisation.value: Colonised by the Dutch (VOC from 1602, then the Dutch East Indies) and occupied by Japan (1942–45). Independence was proclaimed on 17 August 1945 and recognised by the Netherlands on 27 December 1949.

riseSignals.value: Nationalist movements from 1908, the 1928 Youth Pledge, the independence proclamation (1945) and victory in the National Revolution (1949).

peakPeriod.value: Ongoing. Strong economic performance since 2007, and democratisation since 1998.

declineSignals.value: Not in decline. Challenges named in the sources: corruption, separatist conflicts, natural disasters, deforestation and concerns about democratic quality.

outcome.value: Ongoing: a presidential republic and Southeast Asia’s largest economy (HDI 0.728, “high”, 2023).

sources.value: Official statistics and modern histories, checked against Wikipedia (“Indonesia” and “History of Indonesia”) on 5 Nov 2026, though later article sections were only summarised. See also Ricklefs (2008).

overallCertainty.value: High for dates and statistics. The 1965–66 death toll (500,000 to about 1 million), the East Timor occupation and the status of Papua are sensitive and debated, so they are presented with the sources’ own neutral wording.
